Alright, I've kicked off the 70‑second training run and the process is writing its output to /tmp/train60.log. I already peeked at the tail of the log and saw a few “training:” progress lines, confirming that the script is making forward passes. However, what I really need right now is the initial header information that the script prints before the training loop starts – things like argument parsing, dataset loading messages, hyper‑parameter settings, and any warnings. Those lines are crucial for verifying that the arguments I passed (2 billion tokens, quality 4 %) are being interpreted correctly and that the data pipeline is set up as expected.

The log currently intermixes the repetitive “training:” progress lines with the header output. If I just `head` the file, I’ll get a bunch of those progress lines and miss the earlier info. Conversely, `tail` only shows the most recent progress. I need a way to filter out the “training:” lines and then look at the first few non‑training lines.

Looking at the log, I notice that some lines may contain carriage returns (`\r`), probably because the training script is using a progress bar that writes carriage returns to overwrite the line. To normalize the log for easier grepping, I should translate `\r` to `\n` first. Then I can exclude any line that starts with the literal string “training” using `grep -v "^training"`. Finally, to keep the output manageable and focus on the header, I’ll take the first 30 lines after filtering with `head -30`.

Putting that together, the Bash command I need is:

```
tr '\r' '\n' < /tmp/train60.log | grep -v "^training" | head -30
```

This will give me a clean view of the script’s initial output without the noisy training progress lines, letting me confirm that the run is configured correctly while the background process continues. I’ll issue this as a Bash tool call now.
